summary: Defines an initial set of textual conventions, reusable data type definitions, available to all SNMP MIB modules. It was replaced by RFC 2579.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP management tables are written down in a common notation, and this RFC fixes the names and meanings of the data types that those tables are built from. It also fixes the status column that lets a manager create a row, put it into service and later delete it.

questions: what data types do mib modules share
how do you create a row in an snmp table
subtitle: The shared data types that every SNMP MIB module can use, and the rules for creating and deleting table rows.

tldr.problem: MIB modules written by different vendors need to agree on what a value means, otherwise a management station cannot read one vendor's table and interpret it the same way as another's.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of textual conventions: named types that reuse the primitive types of the Structure of Management Information but add a precise meaning and, where useful, a display format. It also defines the RowStatus convention, a six-value status column that drives the creation, suspension and deletion of table rows.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1903 was a Draft Standard and it obsoleted RFC 1443. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 2579.

sections.title: Why Textual Conventions Exist
sections.content:
A management system contains several nodes, each with a processing entity called an agent that has access to management instrumentation, at least one management station, and a management protocol used to convey management information between the agents and the stations. Operations of the protocol are carried out under an administrative framework that defines authentication, authorization, access control and privacy policies.

Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects residing in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base, or MIB. Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules, and these modules are written using a subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1), called the Structure of Management Information (SMI).

When designing a MIB module it is often useful to define new types similar to those in the SMI. Compared with a type defined in the SMI, each of these new types has a different name, a similar syntax, but a more precise semantics. These newly defined types are termed textual conventions, and they are used for the convenience of humans reading the MIB module. The purpose of this document is to define the initial set of textual conventions available to all MIB modules.

Objects defined using a textual convention are always encoded by the rules that define their primitive type, but they often carry special semantics. An ASN.1 macro, TEXTUAL-CONVENTION, is used to concisely convey the syntax and the semantics of such a convention. For all textual conventions defined in an information module the name must be unique and mnemonic and must not exceed 64 characters, and names longer than 32 characters are not recommended. All names used for the textual conventions defined in all standard information modules must be unique.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB module is a list of managed objects written in a shared notation. A textual convention is a named type that says what a value means, so that two modules built by different people still mean the same thing.

sections.title: The Conventions This RFC Defines
sections.content:
The definitions are given in a module called SNMPv2-TC. DisplayString represents textual information taken from the NVT ASCII character set, with a syntax of OCTET STRING (SIZE (0..255)), so no object using it may exceed 255 characters. PhysAddress represents media- or physical-level addresses, and MacAddress represents an 802 MAC address in canonical order as defined by IEEE 802.1a, with a syntax of OCTET STRING (SIZE (6)).

TruthValue represents a boolean value, with the syntax INTEGER { true(1), false(2) }. TestAndIncr represents integer-valued information used for atomic operations: when a management protocol asks to modify an object instance with this syntax, the new value supplied must match the value the instance currently holds, otherwise the set operation fails with an error of inconsistentValue. If it does match and the current value is the maximum value of 2^31-1 (2147483647 decimal), the value is wrapped to zero, otherwise it is incremented by one. Its syntax is INTEGER (0..2147483647).

AutonomousType represents an independently extensible type identification value, such as a particular sub-tree with further MIB definitions. VariablePointer is a pointer to a specific object instance, for example sysContact.0 or ifInOctets.3, and RowPointer represents a pointer to a conceptual row, its value being the name of the instance of the first accessible columnar object in that row, for example ifIndex.3. The older InstancePointer, which covered both uses, is marked obsolete.

TimeStamp is the value of the sysUpTime object at which a specific occurrence happened. TimeInterval is a period of time measured in units of 0.01 seconds. DateAndTime is a date and time specification carried in 8 or 11 octets: year, month, day, hour, minutes, seconds, deci-seconds, and, when the time is not local, the direction from UTC and the hours and minutes from UTC. The example given for Tuesday May 26, 1992 at 1:30:15 PM EDT is 1992-5-26,13:30:15.0,-4:0.

StorageType describes the memory realization of a conceptual row: a volatile(2) row is lost upon reboot, while a nonVolatile(3), permanent(4) or readOnly(5) row is backed up by stable storage; a permanent row can be changed but not deleted, and a readOnly row can be neither changed nor deleted. TDomain denotes a kind of transport service and TAddress a transport service address; for snmpUDPDomain a TAddress is 6 octets long, the first 4 holding the IP address in network byte order and the last 2 the UDP port.
sections.plainLanguage: The module defines familiar types with precise rules: a text string of up to 255 characters, a six byte hardware address, a true or false value, a counter that only moves forward, a timestamp, and a date and time written in eight or eleven bytes.

sections.title: Creating and Deleting a Table Row
sections.content:
The RowStatus convention is used to manage the creation and deletion of conceptual rows, and is used as the value of the status column of a conceptual row. The status column has six defined values. active means the row is available for use by the managed device. notInService means the row exists in the agent but is not available for use. notReady means the row exists but is missing information needed to make it available. createAndWait and createAndGo are supplied by a management station that wishes to create a new row, with createAndGo setting the status to active automatically. destroy is supplied to delete all of the instances associated with an existing row.

Five of the six values may be specified in a set operation, but only three are returned by a retrieval: notReady, notInService and active. Setting the status column to createAndGo when it does not yet exist returns noError and moves the row to active, or inconsistentValue if the agent cannot supply the values the row needs. Setting it to createAndWait creates the row and sets the status to notInService or notReady, depending on the information available.

Creating a row takes four interactions. First the management station selects an instance identifier, which is semantically significant in some tables and merely a label in others. Second the station creates the row, either in one transaction with createAndGo or in a negotiated set of interactions with createAndWait. Third the station initializes the objects for which the agent supplies no default, using a get operation on every column: a value returned means the agent has one, noSuchInstance means the station must supply a value, and noSuchObject means the agent does not implement that object type at all. Fourth the station sets the status column to active, which succeeds with noError if the agent has enough information, and otherwise fails with inconsistentValue.

A row that is left in notInService or notReady consumes resources indefinitely, so the agent must remove conceptual rows that stay in either state for an abnormally long period. The DESCRIPTION clause of the status column should say what that period is, and in the absence of such information the RFC suggests approximately 5 minutes. When a row is active the management station may set the status to notInService to take it out of service, and to destroy to delete it, which removes all instances associated with the row immediately.
sections.plainLanguage: Every row in a management table has a status column with six possible values. The manager sets that column to create, use or delete the row, and the agent reports back whether the row is in use, ready but idle, or missing information it needs.

sections.title: The Clauses of a Textual Convention
sections.content:
The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro conveys the syntax and semantics of a convention, and its expansion happens during implementation rather than at run time. A convention has four clauses. The SYNTAX clause must be present and defines the abstract data structure, which must be one of the alternatives in the ObjectSyntax CHOICE or the BITS construct. The STATUS clause must be present and says whether the definition is current or historic: current and obsolete are self-explanatory, and deprecated means the definition is obsolete but an implementor may want to support it to work with older implementations. The DESCRIPTION clause must be present and holds the textual definition, providing all the semantic definitions needed for implementation. The REFERENCE clause is optional and gives a cross-reference to a related item in another published work.

The DISPLAY-HINT clause is optional and gives a hint about how the value of an instance might be displayed. It may be present if and only if the syntax has an underlying primitive type of INTEGER or OCTET STRING, though the semantics of a particular syntax can make the hint meaningless, as with Counter32.

For an INTEGER, the hint has two parts. The first is a single character suggesting a display format: x for hexadecimal, d for decimal, o for octal or b for binary. The second part is always omitted for x, o and b, and need not be present for d; if present it starts with a hyphen and is followed by a decimal number giving the implied decimal point. The example given is a convention with the hint d-2 and the syntax INTEGER (0..10000), which suggests that a value of 1234 is rendered as 12.34.

For an OCTET STRING, the hint consists of one or more octet-format specifications, each with five parts: an optional repeat indicator, the octet length, the display format, an optional display separator character, and an optional repeat terminator character. The octets of the value are processed in order of significance, most significant first. A repeat terminator or display separator that would be the last character of the display is suppressed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each convention states its syntax, whether it is current, and a description. It may also give a hint for display, such as showing a value in hexadecimal with a colon after every byte, or placing a decimal point two digits from the end.

sections.title: Security Is Not Discussed Here
sections.content:
The security section of this RFC is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. That is consistent with the rest of the document, which is about the meaning of values rather than about how they are reached or protected.

The security framework itself sits above this document. Operations of the management protocol are carried out under an administrative framework which defines authentication, authorization, access control and privacy policies, as the introduction explains. The conventions defined here, from the RowStatus state machine to the atomic increment of TestAndIncr, are what that framework operates on.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC says nothing about security. Who may read or change a managed object, and how that is checked, is handled by the wider SNMP framework, not by these data types.

viz.caption: THE SIX VALUES OF THE RowStatus COLUMN

items.label: active
items.desc: The row is available for use by the managed device.

items.label: notInService
items.desc: The row exists but is not available for use.

items.label: notReady
items.desc: The row exists but is missing information needed for use.

items.label: createAndGo
items.desc: Create the row and set it to active automatically.

items.label: createAndWait
items.desc: Create the row but do not make it available for use.

items.label: destroy
items.desc: Delete all instances of the row.

viz.caption: THE LIFE OF A CONCEPTUAL ROW
A FEW OF THE CONVENTIONS DEFINED HERE

items.title: DisplayString
items.text: Text in the NVT ASCII character set, up to 255 characters.

items.title: MacAddress
items.text: An 802 MAC address in canonical order, six octets.

items.title: TruthValue
items.text: A boolean, written as INTEGER { true(1), false(2) }.

items.title: TestAndIncr
items.text: A counter that only moves forward, one step at a time.

items.title: TimeInterval
items.text: A period of time measured in units of 0.01 seconds.

items.title: DateAndTime
items.text: A date and time in 8 octets, or 11 with the offset from UTC.
